source_text: Enimvero credens malos esse homines conditione nascendi, illum eis deputavit auctorem, per quem mali operis crimen a Deo bono separaretur; et quoniam erraverat in definitione peccati, ut putaret naturale esse, quod nisi voluntarium esse non potest; consequenter deinceps malae originis malum est commentus artificem; hic religiosior in Deum, contumacior in naturam. Tu vero dicis, malos quidem nasci, sed Deum esse auctorem malorum; contumacior tu in Deum, honorificentior in naturam; haec quippe auctoris maiestate defenditur, auctor autem foeditate operis accusatur.
pass_a_gloss: For indeed believing humans to be evil by the condition of being born, he assigned them that author, through whom the charge of an evil work would be separated from the good God; and since he had erred in the definition of sin, that he would think natural, that which cannot be unless voluntary; consequently thereafter of an evil origin he invented an evil craftsman; here more religious toward God, more contumacious toward nature. You however say, that they are born evil indeed, but that God is the author of evils; more contumacious you toward God, more honorific toward nature; for this is defended by the majesty of the author, but the author is accused by the foulness of the work.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Believing human beings evil by the condition of birth, the Manichaean assigned them an author through whom the blame for the evil work could be kept away from the good God. Since he had erred in the definition of sin, thinking natural something that can only be voluntary, he consistently went on to invent an evil maker for an evil origin. In this he was more reverent toward God and more defiant toward nature. You, however, say that people are born evil, but that God is the author of the evil: you are more defiant toward God and more respectful toward nature. For nature is defended by its author's majesty, while its author is accused by the ugliness of his work.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
